issues.subcategory: Nonrepresentative combined sample treated as population sample
issues.description: The design combines a quota/matched U.S. adult sample with a large sports-wagering oversample, but the analytic plan appears to use the total N for substantive analyses without specifying weighting, stratification, or separate analyses. Sports bettors are likely to differ systematically in gender, age, risk-taking, gambling involvement, substance use, religiosity, and moral attitudes. Treating this combined sample as representative can bias prevalence estimates, correlations, moderation effects, and claims about the U.S. population.
issues.quote: the target sample size will be 2,500 American adults that match nationally representative norms for age and gender. Furthermore, due to the design of the larger project from which this sample is taken, we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically.

issues.subcategory: Insufficient survey weighting and sampling details
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly describes the study as nationally representative, but only states matching to age and gender norms. It does not report whether post-stratification weights will be used, which benchmarks will be applied, how the oversample will be incorporated, response/completion rates, panel recruitment procedures, incentives, eligibility screening, or design effects. These omissions prevent evaluation of population inference and replication.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms.

issues.description: The manuscript says the sample will be over 4,000, but the stated components sum exactly to 4,000. This is minor, but it reflects imprecise reporting of the planned sample size.
issues.quote: This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.description: Most of the manuscript defines moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval and behavioral frequency, but one central statement defines it as the interaction of moral disapproval and severity of consequences. This is a substantive contradiction because frequency and consequences are different constructs and would imply different models, hypotheses, and interpretations.
issues.quote: Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action.

issues.subcategory: Product term does not directly measure moral incongruence
issues.description: The proposed operationalization treats moral incongruence as a statistical interaction between disapproval and frequency. This does not directly measure perceived conflict, distress, value violation, failed self-regulation, or subjective incongruence. A person may disapprove abstractly but not experience distress, or may engage rarely but experience intense conflict. The operationalization therefore may not validly capture the construct invoked by the theory or the ICD-11 caveat about moral distress.
issues.quote: moral incongruence (defined as the interaction of moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior)

issues.description: All moral disapproval constructs are measured with one item. Single items provide no estimate of internal consistency, limited content coverage, and are vulnerable to idiosyncratic interpretation. The same wording may not function equivalently across pornography, alcohol, nicotine, gambling, cannabis, prescription misuse, and illicit drugs, undermining cross-domain comparisons that are central to the paper.
issues.quote: we will include a series of single-item moral disapproval questions that match previous measures of moral disapproval of pornography.

issues.description: The Brief Pornography Screen includes an item explicitly about guilt. Because guilt is closely related to moral disapproval and moral incongruence, using this item within the outcome can mechanically inflate associations between moral disapproval and pornography problems. This threatens the central comparison between pornography and other behaviors.
issues.quote: 5. You continue to use pornography even though you feel guilty about it.

issues.description: The PGSI includes an item about guilt regarding gambling. This overlaps with moral distress and may contaminate the outcome when testing whether moral disapproval predicts gambling problems. It also weakens the planned inference that morality is not relevant to gambling if other PGSI items dilute an explicitly moral/guilt item.
issues.quote: Have you felt guilty about the way you gamble or what happens when you gamble?

issues.subcategory: Unvalidated averaging of heterogeneous ASSIST items
issues.description: The planned modified ASSIST score averages items with different time frames, response formats, and scale ranges: three past-3-month frequency items scored 0–5 and two lifetime/past-3-month items scored 0/3/6. Averaging these assumes equal intervals, equal weights, and a single latent construct despite heterogeneous item content and timing. It departs from validated ASSIST scoring and may produce uninterpretable severity scores.
issues.quote: Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest

issues.subcategory: Unvalidated extension of ASSIST to pornography and gambling
issues.description: The authors acknowledge that the NIDA-ASSIST approach is not validated for pornography or gambling, yet plan to use it for parallel cross-domain analyses. Lack of validation threatens measurement equivalence and interpretability, especially because the primary argument depends on comparing effect sizes across domains.
issues.quote: Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography, given the inclusion of other validated scales to assess these outcomes (see below), including them within the NIDA-ASSIST will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses.

issues.subcategory: Outcomes do not consistently measure self-perceived addiction
issues.description: The theoretical claims focus on self-perceived feelings of addiction, but several outcomes are symptom/risk screens or consequence scales rather than direct measures of perceived addiction. PGSI, BPS, and modified ASSIST assess urges, consequences, failed control, and impairment, not necessarily self-labeling as addicted. This mismatch limits the ability to test claims about morality shaping self-perceived addiction.
issues.quote: problem gambling behavior will be measured using the Problem Gambling Severity Index

issues.subcategory: Mismatched time frames across predictors and outcomes
issues.description: Behavior frequency is assessed over the past 12 months, ASSIST problems over the past 3 months plus lifetime/past-3-month items, pornography symptoms over 6 months, gambling symptoms over 12 months, and moral disapproval apparently at the time of survey. These nonparallel time frames can obscure temporal ordering and create measurement mismatch in the proposed interactions.
issues.quote: Participants will be asked how often they have engaged in the behavior over the past 12 months using the same 6-point scale described above

issues.description: The manuscript says that only past-year users will complete further problematic-use measures, but later says problematic-use and moral-disapproval measures will be administered to all participants regardless of engagement. This directly affects sample sizes, missingness, range restriction, definition of analytic subsets, and interpretation of moral incongruence among abstainers versus users.
issues.quote: Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use. | That is, we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample.

issues.description: The text describes pornography frequency as coded 1–6 with 1 = never, whereas the supplemental materials use 0–5 with 0 = never. The text also defines user inclusion as scores > 1, which would exclude people reporting once or twice if the 1–6 coding is used and would be wrong under 0–5 coding. This affects inclusion criteria and all interaction terms.
issues.quote: participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day)

issues.description: The methods state that BPS responses range from 0 to 2, but the supplemental instrument codes the same responses as 0, 2, and 4. This changes total scores and effect sizes and makes replication impossible unless clarified.
issues.quote: on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent PGSI scoring and nonstandard scoring
issues.description: The methods state the PGSI uses a 0–3 scale and that responses will be averaged, whereas the supplemental materials code options as 0, 2, 4, and 5. Standard PGSI scoring is typically 0–3 summed. The proposed scoring inconsistency can alter distributions, reliability, thresholds, and regression coefficients.
issues.quote: on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged.

issues.description: The manuscript says gambling frequency will be measured with a single item, but then says an average across gambling behaviors will be taken. The supplemental materials appear to include only one general gambling item. This ambiguity matters because a single global frequency item and an average across multiple activities have different meanings and psychometric properties.
issues.quote: We will assess gambling frequency using a single item. | To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.

issues.description: The male-specific alcohol item asks about more than five drinks, but the response-row label says more than four drinks. This could confuse respondents or coders and undermines accurate assessment of sex-specific binge drinking frequency.
issues.quote:
IF GENDER = MAN

In the past year, how often have you had more than 5 drinks on one occasion?

issues.description: The text says tobacco and non-tobacco nicotine will be included as separate substances in the averaged problematic-use scores, but the questionnaire and other sections combine all tobacco/nicotine products into one item. This changes the number of outcomes and makes the planned analyses unclear.
issues.quote: Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest (i.e., alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, cannabis).

issues.description: The analytic plan first states an equivalence region based on δ = .27, but later says the equivalence region is δ = |.11|. These are very different thresholds; conclusions about practical equivalence could change depending on which is used. This is a critical preregistration error because equivalence testing is central to the hypotheses.
issues.quote: with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27.

issues.subcategory: Noncomparable standardized interaction coefficients across domains
issues.description: The plan uses a standardized interaction coefficient from pornography studies as the SESOI for gambling and substance outcomes. Standardized interaction effects depend on the distributions and variances of the predictor, moderator, product term, and outcome, which differ markedly across behaviors and oversampled groups. This undermines the claim that effects are comparable or practically equivalent across domains.
issues.quote: Should the confidence interval for the observed standardized effect of the interaction for moral disapproval of a behavior and frequency of that behavior fall fully within our equivalence region

issues.subcategory: No multiplicity control for primary hypothesis tests
issues.description: The authors plan multiple moderation analyses and equivalence tests across behaviors and outcomes but only mention Holm adjustment for bivariate correlations, not for the confirmatory tests. The probability of false positives or selective interpretation is inflated, especially because the central conclusion depends on one domain showing an effect while several others do not.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest

issues.subcategory: Uniqueness inferred from significant versus nonsignificant effects
issues.description: The manuscript proposes to conclude that moral incongruence is unique to pornography if the pornography interaction is significant and other interactions are null/equivalent. However, differences in significance do not establish differences between effects. The study needs direct statistical comparisons of interaction effects across domains, ideally in a unified multilevel or seemingly unrelated framework accounting for within-person dependence.
issues.quote: should we find that moral incongruence—defined as the interaction between moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior—only predicts self-reported problematic use of pornography, then this work would provide strong evidence

issues.subcategory: Power analysis does not address equivalence testing or survey design
issues.description: The power analysis is based on ordinary regression detection of f2 using simple effective Ns. It does not evaluate power for equivalence tests, account for survey weights/design effects, oversampling, skewed and zero-inflated outcomes, or the precision of interaction estimates under uneven distributions of moral disapproval and use frequency. Thus, stated power may be overly optimistic.
issues.quote: using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2009), we conducted a power analysis to determine the sample size needed to reliably detect our smallest effect of interest (f2 = .015)

issues.description: The authors acknowledge that prescription drug misuse and illicit drug analyses may be underpowered for the planned SESOI. Because these domains are central to the claim that moral incongruence does not generalize to substances, inadequate power undermines confirmatory conclusions for those outcomes.
issues.quote: in the case of illicit drug use (prevalence estimated at 6%-12% of the population) and prescription drug misuse (prevalence estimated at 3.5% of the population), it is possible, if not probable, that our final sample sizes will fall below the minimum size required to detect effects that small

issues.subcategory: Post hoc relaxed equivalence criterion for underpowered analyses
issues.description: When power is insufficient to test equivalence to the prespecified small SESOI, the authors propose a broader alternative equivalence region. This changes the inferential target from practical null to merely smaller than a prior pornography effect, weakening hypothesis tests while still allowing supportive language. Such contingency rules should be clearly labeled exploratory and should not be used to confirm the original null hypotheses.
issues.quote: Should we lack power to sufficient test equivalence with null effects for the above behaviors, we will adjust analyses accordingly.

issues.description: The plan proposes redefining the equivalence region using the observed lower bound of the pornography interaction confidence interval. This makes the threshold data-dependent and can bias conclusions about whether other effects are meaningfully smaller than the pornography effect.
issues.quote: we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome.

issues.description: The plan says alternative analyses will be conducted if assumptions are substantially violated but does not define what counts as substantial violation, which alternative models will be used, or how conflicting results will be adjudicated. This creates researcher degrees of freedom in a registered report.
issues.quote: in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate.

issues.subcategory: Ambiguous primary outcomes for pornography and gambling
issues.description: Pornography and gambling are each assessed with both validated scales and modified ASSIST items, but the hypotheses and analytic plan do not clearly specify which outcome is primary for confirmatory inference. This ambiguity permits selective emphasis if BPS/PGSI and modified ASSIST results diverge.
issues.quote:
Pornography Use | Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items
Gambling Behavior | Problem Gambling Severity Index and modified NIDA-ASSIST items

issues.subcategory: OLS applied to ordinal and bounded variables without adequate model specification
issues.description: The proposed analyses use linear regression with ordinal frequency predictors, single-item Likert moderators, and bounded symptom outcomes that are likely skewed and zero-inflated. Treating unequal ordinal categories such as never, monthly, weekly, daily, and more than once per day as interval-scaled can distort interactions. The plan does not prespecify ordinal, count, zero-inflated, or robust alternatives.
issues.quote: we will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function in the stats package for R statistical software

issues.description: Holm adjustment modifies p-values or significance thresholds, not test statistics. This is a minor statistical reporting error but suggests imprecision in the planned reporting of correlations.
issues.quote: Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics using the psych package.

issues.description: The manuscript assumes no unplanned missingness because YouGov will collect the data. This is not a missing-data strategy. Panel covariates, sensitive-behavior items, skip logic, breakoffs, refusals, and vendor-provided data can still produce missingness. The plan does not specify listwise deletion, imputation, weighting adjustments, or handling of missing covariates/outcomes.
issues.quote: Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.description: The authors rely on YouGov's proprietary quality control and plan no additional exclusions for inattentive or invalid responding. Because the study uses online self-report of sensitive and illegal behaviors, lack of transparent attention checks, speeding criteria, duplicate prevention, consistency checks, and exclusion rules threatens data validity and replicability.
issues.quote: certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed as a part of their data collection process based on their proprietary data collection standards. Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding.

issues.subcategory: Causal language from cross-sectional observational data
issues.description: The manuscript uses language implying influence, contribution, and effects of moral incongruence on addiction perceptions. The proposed study is cross-sectional and observational, so it cannot establish temporal precedence or rule out reverse causation, such as problematic use increasing guilt or moral disapproval. The limitations section notes cross-sectional design, but causal phrasing remains central to hypotheses and implications.
issues.quote: we seek to establish whether moral incongruence (defined as the interaction of moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior) influences self-perceived feelings of addiction

issues.description: The planned covariates are limited to religiousness, age, and gender. Many plausible confounders could affect both moral disapproval and self-reported addiction/problems, including psychological distress, shame proneness, social desirability, political ideology, denomination, legal context, relationship status, education, race/ethnicity, income, treatment history, and baseline severity. Without addressing these, regression coefficients cannot support causal or mechanistic claims.
issues.quote: we intend on including religiousness, age, and gender as covariates

issues.subcategory: Alcohol frequency measure poorly matched to alcohol use disorder risk
issues.description: The authors intentionally use general drinking frequency rather than heavy-drinking frequency for the main alcohol frequency predictor. Frequency of any alcohol use does not capture quantity, binge drinking, intoxication, or loss of control, and moral disapproval of “drinking alcohol” may differ from moral disapproval of drunkenness or harmful drinking. This weakens the alcohol comparison with pornography and gambling.
issues.quote: for the sake of the present study, we will look at alcohol frequency more generally (i.e., asking participants how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed).

issues.description: The study collapses heterogeneous products and behaviors into broad categories such as tobacco/nicotine products and illegal/illicit drugs. These categories differ in legality, health risk, social stigma, typical frequency, route of administration, dependence liability, and moral meaning. Broad grouping may obscure or create associations and undermines comparability across substances.
issues.quote: smoked tobacco products, e-cigarettes/vapes, and smokeless tobacco products are all subsumed by our single question on tobacco/nicotine.

issues.subcategory: Moral disapproval confounded with illegality and stigmatizing labels
issues.description: Items for prescription drug misuse and illicit drugs include morally and legally loaded wording such as non-medical reasons and illegal/illicit. Agreement may reflect legality, perceived harm, stigma, or semantic agreement that illegal behavior is wrong rather than personal moral incongruence. This threatens construct validity for substance comparisons.
issues.quote: I believe that using prescription drugs for non-medical reasons is morally wrong | I believe that using illegal/illicit drugs is morally wrong.

issues.description: The analysis codes gender as male versus not-male, collapsing women and nonbinary or other gender-diverse respondents. This may obscure gender differences relevant to pornography, gambling, substance use, and moral disapproval, and it is inconsistent with nuanced measurement of gender in a representative sample.
issues.quote: gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male)

issues.description: The title and limitations refer to a registered or preregistered design, but the manuscript does not provide a registry link, time stamp, versioned analysis script, planned decision rules for all outcomes, or criteria for deviations. For a registered report, these details are necessary to evaluate whether hypotheses and analyses are fixed before data access.
issues.quote: Although the proposed work has many strengths (nationally representative sample, pre-registered design, rigorous statistical evaluation of hypotheses)

issues.subcategory: Insufficient participant recruitment and ethics details
issues.description: The methods do not describe consent procedures, compensation, survey duration, eligibility criteria beyond adulthood and sports wagering for the oversample, exclusion of prior panel participation, IRB/ethics approval, or data access timing. These details are necessary for evaluating participant protection and replicability.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited in late March of 2022 as a part of a larger study of sports wagering behaviors in the American populace funded by the International Center for Responsible Gaming.

issues.description: The manuscript frames CSBD and pornography problems as addictions alongside recognized substance and gambling disorders. CSBD is classified in ICD-11 as an impulse-control disorder, and pornography addiction is not a recognized diagnosis. This framing may overextend addiction terminology and complicate interpretation of comparisons with recognized addictive disorders.
issues.quote: if moral incongruence (the interaction of behavioral frequency and moral disapproval of a behavior) is uniquely related to sexual behavior, or if it generalizes to other addictions as well.

issues.subcategory: Overinterpretation of implications for ICD-11 diagnostic criteria
issues.description: The proposed population survey of self-reported symptoms cannot validate or invalidate the ICD-11 diagnostic caveat for CSBD. The caveat concerns clinical diagnosis and differential diagnosis, whereas this study uses cross-sectional self-report in a largely nonclinical sample. Even if moral incongruence is uniquely associated with pornography self-reports, that would not directly establish the diagnostic validity of the ICD-11 criterion.
issues.quote: there would be additional evidence supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11 for CSBD.

issues.subcategory: Sexual behavior conclusions based almost entirely on solitary pornography use
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly discusses sexual behavior and CSBD broadly, but the empirical measures focus on pornography viewed alone and a pornography-specific screen. Other CSBD-relevant behaviors, such as partnered sexual behavior, casual sex, paid sex, compulsive masturbation, or cybersex interactions, are not assessed. Findings therefore cannot be generalized to sexual behavior or CSBD as a whole.
issues.quote: Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner)

issues.description: The analytic plan says there will be eight moderation analyses corresponding to eight target behaviors/variables, but the listed domains are seven: pornography, gambling, alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, prescription drug misuse, and illicit drug use. It is unclear whether the eighth analysis is a second pornography or gambling outcome, and if so which analyses are confirmatory.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest, with pornography and gambling assessed using the validate measures of problematic use

issues.subcategory: Failure to account for within-person dependence across behaviors
issues.description: The same participants provide reports for multiple behaviors and substances, but the plan analyzes each outcome separately. Cross-domain conclusions about uniqueness would be strengthened by models that account for within-person correlations and directly compare effects. Ignoring dependence can lead to inefficient or misleading comparisons of moral incongruence across domains.
issues.quote: In each analysis, moral disapproval of the behavior in question (pornography use, gambling, alcohol use, nicotine use, cannabis use, prescription drug misuse, and illicit drug use) will be tested as a moderator

issues.subcategory: Sensitive and illegal behavior self-report without validity safeguards
issues.description: The study relies on self-reported pornography use, gambling, prescription misuse, and illicit drug use, but does not describe protections or methods to reduce underreporting, such as anonymity assurances, privacy checks, indirect questioning, social desirability assessment, or validity checks. Differential underreporting may be correlated with moral disapproval, biasing the focal interactions.
issues.quote:
Past Year Substance Use

In the past year, how often have you used the following?
